Second, the account's ladder (chores first, the avoider at step 4) becomes: avoider first, classification in parallel, pilot after. Grounds: the objection's c1 and o3 — withdrawal is the distinctive feature of this situation, and thin material licenses parallel probes rather than a fixed sequence. I keep the threshold with one addition: a rough time-box (a few weeks, or one full rotation of the changing schedules), because otherwise "not indefinitely deferred" has no operational meaning. The specific length is arbitrary and I am stating it as such.

The objection's o4 stays attached to the reordering. Neither caution is resolvable from the material available.

What stays open. Work on the problem using the material actually exposed in this request and your background knowledge. The problem has no supplied answer key or scoring rule. Claims, criticisms and methods are fallible. Do not invent a source, an observation, an earlier event, or a dependency to fill a field. A missing view says what you can currently see; it does not establish what happened earlier. Return a JSON object with exactly two independently authored string fields: body and commitments. Body is your public prose contribution. Commitments says what taking your contribution up would involve. An empty commitment surface is allowed when none can be identified. Do not repeat the body wholesale into commitments.

Use FCL-1 for the commitment surface, encoded as a JSON document inside the commitments string: {"language":"FCL-1","records":[...],"uptake":[...]}. Each record has unique local id, type (claim|commitment|objection|use|problem), and text (unrestricted prose). Optional prose fields: scope, action, consequence, grounds, bearing. Optional arrays of references: target, depends, mentions, revises, withdraws. References are local IDs or exposed-artifact-label#local-ID; do not invent hidden IDs. A commitment proposes a scoped use, action, application or consequence; an objection alleges a defect whose bearing can itself be criticized; a use proposes an uptake or response; a problem states an unresolved question. depends asserts reliance; mentions only locates material. uptake lists the records you currently propose to use, not certified truths. No record type or optional field must be present. Empty records and uptake are allowed. Express uncertainty or an unrepresentable relation in prose rather than inventing a relation. The body remains unrestricted prose.

Return one JSON object with exactly two string fields: "body" and "commitments". Write the actual commitments separately; do not copy the body into that field as a storage shortcut.

## Node response

Continue the inquiry in light of the account, criticism and alternative. Decide what to use, leave open, revise or reject, and explain your grounds where they matter.

## Original problem

I share a flat with two friends. We keep arguing about ordinary household chores. Sometimes we agree on who will do something, but later we disagree about what the agreement meant. Our work schedules change, and one friend has started avoiding the conversations. What should I do?

## Selected input account

Source account: daily/mini_fcl/cycle-1/account; selected view: both
Artifact: cd6e3e2f307e0dac79543de9bed087db4ee7dcd40b3d989d3c6d4b02057d8b99
Original body SHA256: 360ee14fa7545c90cadf79c7d2fe9c157faf470d6368504b06768e36e0d13c79
Original commitments SHA256: bd7faa10242d5841c8063c7a0919a20706c658c4a2054a5729caeacbc3cd04c8
Delivery: COMPLETE; envelope: AUTHORED
BODY
The problem as posed is practical, and the material is thin: three flatmates, recurring disputes about ordinary chores, agreements that later turn out to have been understood differently, changing work schedules, and one friend withdrawing from the conversation. There is also a first-fork note saying the prior source was absent in the first template invocation, so there is no earlier account to inherit or revise against. I should not pretend to know what was said in prior conversations, what the chores are, who is avoiding whom, or why.

The most useful thing to conjecture is that the repeated disagreement is not primarily about willingness. Two people can agree that the dishes should be done and still disagree later about whether the agreement meant "by tonight," "before the kitchen is used again," or "on your turn." That is an ambiguity problem, not a motivation problem. Changing schedules make any fixed arrangement fragile, and avoidance is a predictable response when each conversation feels like relitigating fault. So the working hypothesis is: the household is running on spoken agreements with unstated specifications, and the cost of that ambiguity has become high enough that one participant is exiting the conversation rather than re-entering it.

A second, less certain hypothesis is that the avoidance is about the form of the conversations rather than the chores. If past talks ended in grievance or in one person doing most of the negotiating work, withdrawal is a sensible local strategy. I cannot tell from the material whether that is happening.

What I would try, roughly in order:

1. Separate the recurring disputes into the smallest repeated cases (e.g. kitchen surfaces, bins, bathroom, shared shopping). Do not start with a general talk about fairness; start with two or three concrete items that actually recur.

2. For each item, write down three things in a shared note: what counts as done, when it counts as done, and what happens when someone cannot do it. The third column matters because schedules change. "If you cannot do it by the agreed time, say so the day before and the other two decide" is different from "whoever notices does it."

3. Treat the written note as a draft, not a contract. Its purpose is to surface disagreement while it is still about a chore rather than about a person. If a written version feels too formal, a shared message thread or a note on the fridge does the same work with less ceremony.

4. Approach the friend who is avoiding the conversations separately and with a smaller ask. Not "we need to talk about the house," which invites the same argument, but "I noticed you've been quiet about this; I'd rather not keep pushing it in the group. Can we spend ten minutes on just the bins and the kitchen?" Give that person an easier entry point, and accept a lower-commitment role at first.

5. If the avoidance continues after one or two low-pressure attempts, stop treating it as a scheduling problem. Then the question becomes whether the living arrangement itself still works. That is a larger decision and should not be forced by a chore dispute, but it should not be indefinitely deferred either.

What I would avoid: a single big meeting intended to settle everything, moral language about "pulling weight," and counting instances as evidence in the moment. Those tend to convert a specification problem into a character dispute, which is exactly the shape the current disagreement already has.

I should be clear about what this is not. It is not a claim that the withdrawing friend is acting in good faith; I do not know. It is not a claim that the others are blameless. It is not a claim that written agreements work for every household. It is a conjecture that a large share of the recurring friction is ambiguity under shifting schedules, and that the ambiguity is addressable independently of who is right about any particular past disagreement. The strongest test of that conjecture is whether two or three concrete items, specified more tightly, stop recurring. If they do not, the hypothesis is wrong and the problem is probably about the relationship or the living arrangement rather than the chores.
COMMITMENTS

## Selected input objection

Source objection: daily/mini_fcl/cycle-1/objection; selected view: both
Artifact: 406eff787391049a53c08a1fa638c1576c4a54c65be4bdde122593deb25fdbbe
Original body SHA256: 4db1a45a95ad1b9ef0dda40057368e6b2dc5c80bf57fed25aec7d5d3f0755365
Original commitments SHA256: 063f3d88f0f47fcd5c20059a02d098f515a274f6baf927c6b6646f18516f46e8
Delivery: COMPLETE; envelope: AUTHORED
BODY
I want to press on the account's central move: reframing the conflict as
a specification problem rather than a motivation or fairness problem.
That reframing is doing a lot of work, and the material does not
obviously support it.

Consider what the problem statement actually reports. Three flatmates
argue about ordinary chores. Sometimes they agree who will do something,
then later disagree about what the agreement meant. Schedules change.
One person has started avoiding the conversations. The account reads the
recurring "later disagreement about what it meant" as evidence of
ambiguity in the agreements. But the same observation is equally
consistent with a different reading: the agreement was clear enough, and
the later dispute is about whether the terms still bind given changed
circumstances, or about who has standing to enforce them. "You said
you'd do the bins" / "yes, and then my shift changed" is not necessarily
a semantics problem. It can be a renegotiation problem, or a legitimacy
problem.

The account acknowledges this in o1 but then treats the ambiguity
hypothesis as the working one and downweights the alternatives. That is
a defensible starting point if you have to pick one, but the account's
own diagnostic step - try two or three concrete items and see if
recurrence falls - is weaker than it looks, because a specification move
can reduce friction while the underlying driver is load imbalance or
resentment. Tighter specs on a lopsided arrangement are still a lopsided
arrangement, just with clearer paperwork. Falling recurrence would be
consistent with the ambiguity hypothesis, but the alternative hypotheses
predict a different pattern: recurrence might drop on the specified
items and reappear as new complaint items, or drop for a while and then
return when circumstances change again. The account's test does not
distinguish these.

There is also a phrasing issue worth flagging. The account says the
problem as posed is "practical" and the material is "thin." Those are
the author's characterizations, not features of the situation. Calling
the material thin is fine as a caution, but the account then uses the
thinness to license a fair bit of construction (the three-column spec,
the low-pressure approach to the withdrawing friend, the step-5
threshold). Thin material supports tentative proposals; it does not
support sequencing those proposals as if the ambiguity reading had
already earned its place at the front.

The account's most useful move is probably the one it treats as
secondary: that the avoidance may be about the form of the conversations
rather than the chores. That deserves to be nearer the front, because it
is the part of the situation that is genuinely distinctive and that the
specific-negotiation advice does not address. A tight spec on bins does
not get a withdrawn flatmate back into the room. The account half-sees
this in c3 and step 4, but the overall frame still centers the chores.

What I would not claim: that the ambiguity hypothesis is wrong. I cannot
tell from the material. My objection is to the ordering and to the
test's strength, not to the hypothesis's plausibility. If the account
were rewritten with the conversational-form reading as the first
hypothesis and the spec move as one of several probes, I would have less
to say against it.
COMMITMENTS

## Selected input rival

Source rival: daily/mini_fcl/cycle-1/rival; selected view: both
Artifact: a6a817c086b877f919ae3a927d532ce46d007e49969962bcc613eb541fae0644
Original body SHA256: ca39bb97ac2b9415bd3d1cf52b318950797849095c017c0c99d3012020e45312
Original commitments SHA256: 5d08a79220b70ce3a31f83a3270998bbdd7ef386b3fb3297b5c883c067f05000
Delivery: COMPLETE; envelope: AUTHORED
BODY
The rival framing I want to try is not another chore protocol. It is the question of what the agreements were for.

The selected account treats the trouble as ambiguity in specifications: agreements lack criteria for done-ness and timing, schedules shift, so friction recurs. That is a good hypothesis as far as it goes, and I have no material that contradicts it. But it quietly assumes that everyone wanted a specification. The avoidance suggests the opposite for at least one flatmate. A person can stay away from a conversation not because the terms are vague but because any settled term would feel like a binding owed to people they live with, and that is a different problem from the one the selected account addresses.

So the rival pose is: maybe the disputes are not failing negotiations about tasks. Maybe they are negotiations about whether the flat is a unit with obligations or three private lives sharing fixtures. Under that reading, writing down "what counts as done" is not neutral — it is one side of a contested question, enacted without having settled it. Shifting schedules are then not merely a complication; they are the fact that makes the unit-reading feel coercive to the person who is withdrawing.

I cannot tell which reading is right from the material. What I can do is name a test that distinguishes them rather than assuming one. The selected account's test is whether tightened specifications stop recurrences. Mine adds a second: when specifications are proposed, does the withdrawing flatmate engage with their content or pull back from the proposal itself? Content-engagement supports the ambiguity reading. Pullback from the very idea of a written arrangement supports the unit-versus-privacy reading.

Roughly what I would do differently from the selected account:

1. Do not open with a shared note. Open by asking the two flatmates, separately, what they think the flat is — a shared project with mutual obligations, or three lives that happen to overlap in a kitchen. Do not ask it as a survey; ask it as a real disagreement I am willing to hear out.

2. If the answers diverge, treat that as the actual dispute, and treat the chores as the surface where it keeps surfacing. Chore rules can then be framed as a truce between two readings rather than as a correct specification that one side has been failing to meet.

3. Consider an arrangement that does not require agreement on meaning: individually-owned zones, or a rotation with a default outcome that nobody has to negotiate in the moment (for example, each person is responsible for a defined zone and the group does not audit it). This trades efficiency for reduced exposure, which is what a privacy-reading flatmate may actually want.

4. If one or both flatmates reject even truce-shaped arrangements, stop optimizing chores and start asking whether the lease and living arrangement still fit. That is not a chore failure.

What I am not claiming: that the withdrawing flatmate is the reasonable one, that written rules are coercive in general, or that the ambiguity reading is wrong. The selected account's diagnosis may well be correct and mine may simply add a second axis. The point of the rival is to make the second axis visible, because a plan that only addresses ambiguity will keep running into a wall if the disagreement is about what kind of household this is.
